The person who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1954 with Max Born was **Walther Bothe**.

Walther Bothe was born in **Rochlitz, Germany** (in the German Empire at the time).

Max Born shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics with Walther Bothe "for their fundamental research in quantum mechanics, especially for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction" and "for the coincidence method and his discoveries made therewith," respectively.

Enders, Thomas H. Weller and Frederick C. Robbins; and Dr Anders Österling spoke for the absent Nobel Laureate in Literature, Ernest Hemingway; John C. Cabot, United States Ambassador to Sweden, received the Nobel Prize on behalf of Mr Hemingway.

In 1954, physicist Max Born received the Nobel Prize in Physics, sharing the honor with Walther Bothe for their groundbreaking contributions to quantum mechanics. At the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm, Born delivered a heartfelt and thought-provoking speech that remains timeless in its relevance.
Born began by expressing profound gratitude for the recognition, emphasizing the collective spirit of science:
"We are a great fellowship, men of all nations seeking after the truth."
This statement highlighted the global and collaborative essence of scientific exploration—a principle he saw endangered by the growing politicization of science.
Born championed the idea that science thrives on freedom, cautioning against the subjugation of scientific research to political agendas. He lamented barriers of "fear and suspicion" that hindered collaboration among scientists, urging the world to preserve the liberty that allows ideas to flourish.
The Shift in Thinking: From Determinism to Probability
Born's most profound reflections came when he addressed the transformative nature of his work. At the end of the 19th century, scientists viewed the universe as a perfect machine governed by deterministic laws. If one knew the universe's state at a given moment, they believed, its future could be predicted with certainty.

But the 20th century shattered this illusion. Observations in atomic and cosmic realms revealed phenomena that defied the deterministic framework. Born's contributions to the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics introduced a paradigm where chance and freedom replaced rigid determinism.
"A philosophy in which the notions of chance and freedom are fundamental seems to me preferable to the almost inhuman determinism of the previous epoch."
This shift was not born out of speculation but forced upon science by the observed realities of nature—a testament to science's ability to adapt and evolve in pursuit of truth.
A Personal Touch
Born concluded his speech with a touching anecdote. Over 40 years earlier, he and his wife had honeymooned in Sweden, staying in Drottningholm. Returning now as a Nobel laureate was a full-circle moment filled with gratitude and nostalgia.
He also expressed regret over the absence of his co-laureate, Walther Bothe, who was unwell, and extended heartfelt wishes for his recovery—a reminder of the humility and camaraderie that defined Born's character.
Why This Speech Still Resonates
Max Born’s reflections are more than a historical artifact—they are a powerful reminder of the principles underpinning science. His advocacy for freedom, collaboration, and the courage to challenge established ideas remains vital in an age where science continues to shape human thought and endeavor.
As Born so eloquently said:
"The mind can grow and bear fruit only in freedom."
His words inspire us to honor the spirit of discovery, embrace uncertainty, and work together across boundaries in the unending quest for truth.

**Max Born** (German:[[ˈmaks ˈbɔʁn]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")ⓘ; 11 December 1882 – 5 January 1970) was a German–British theoretical physicist who was instrumental in the development of quantum mechanics. He also made contributions to solid-state physics and optics, and supervised the work of a number of notable physicists in the 1920s and 1930s. He shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics with Walther Bothe "for his fundamental research in quantum mechanics, especially for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Born#cite_note-Nobel_Prize-3)
Born entered the University of Göttingen in 1904, where he met the three renowned mathematicians Felix Klein, David Hilbert, and Hermann Minkowski. He wrote his [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") thesis on the subject of the stability of elastic wires and tapes, winning the university's Philosophy Faculty Prize. In 1905, he began researching special relativity with Minkowski, and subsequently wrote his habilitation thesis on the Thomson model of the atom. In 1954, physicist Max Born received the Nobel Prize in Physics, sharing the honor with Walther Bothe for their groundbreaking contributions to quantum mechanics. At the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm, Born delivered a heartfelt and thought-provoking speech that remains timeless in its relevance.
Born began by expressing profound gratitude for the recognition, emphasizing the collective spirit of science:
"We are a great fellowship, men of all nations seeking after the truth."
This statement highlighted the global and collaborative essence of scientific exploration—a principle he saw endangered by the growing politicization of science.
Born championed the idea that science thrives on freedom, cautioning against the subjugation of scientific research to political agendas. He lamented barriers of "fear and suspicion" that hindered collaboration among scientists, urging the world to preserve the liberty that allows ideas to flourish.
The Shift in Thinking: From Determinism to Probability
Born's most profound reflections came when he addressed the transformative nature of his work. At the end of the 19th century, scientists viewed the universe as a perfect machine governed by deterministic laws. If one knew the universe's state at a given moment, they believed, its future could be predicted with certainty.

But the 20th century shattered this illusion. Observations in atomic and cosmic realms revealed phenomena that defied the deterministic framework. Born's contributions to the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics introduced a paradigm where chance and freedom replaced rigid determinism.
"A philosophy in which the notions of chance and freedom are fundamental seems to me preferable to the almost inhuman determinism of the previous epoch."
This shift was not born out of speculation but forced upon science by the observed realities of nature—a testament to science's ability to adapt and evolve in pursuit of truth.
A Personal Touch
Born concluded his speech with a touching anecdote. Over 40 years earlier, he and his wife had honeymooned in Sweden, staying in Drottningholm. Returning now as a Nobel laureate was a full-circle moment filled with gratitude and nostalgia.
He also expressed regret over the absence of his co-laureate, Walther Bothe, who was unwell, and extended heartfelt wishes for his recovery—a reminder of the humility and camaraderie that defined Born's character.
Why This Speech Still Resonates
Max Born’s reflections are more than a historical artifact—they are a powerful reminder of the principles underpinning science. His advocacy for freedom, collaboration, and the courage to challenge established ideas remains vital in an age where science continues to shape human thought and endeavor.
As Born so eloquently said:
"The mind can grow and bear fruit only in freedom."
His words inspire us to honor the spirit of discovery, embrace uncertainty, and work together across boundaries in the unending quest for truth.

**Max Born** (German:[[ˈmaks ˈbɔʁn]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")ⓘ; 11 December 1882 – 5 January 1970) was a German–British theoretical physicist who was instrumental in the development of quantum mechanics. He also made contributions to solid-state physics and optics, and supervised the work of a number of notable physicists in the 1920s and 1930s. He shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics with Walther Bothe "for his fundamental research in quantum mechanics, especially for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Born#cite_note-Nobel_Prize-3)
Born entered the University of Göttingen in 1904, where he met the three renowned mathematicians Felix Klein, David Hilbert, and Hermann Minkowski. He wrote his [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") thesis on the subject of the stability of elastic wires and tapes, winning the university's Philosophy Faculty Prize. In 1905, he began researching special relativity with Minkowski, and subsequently wrote his habilitation thesis on the Thomson model of the atom. A chance meeting with Fritz Haber in Berlin in 1918 led to discussion of how an ionic compound is formed when a metal reacts with a halogen, which is now known as the Born–Haber cycle.
During World War I, Born was originally placed as a radio operator, but his specialist knowledge led to his being moved to research duties on sound ranging. In 1921 Born returned to Göttingen, where he arranged another chair for his long-time friend and colleague James Franck. Under Born, Göttingen became one of the world's foremost centres for physics. In 1925, Born and Werner Heisenberg formulated the matrix mechanics representation of quantum mechanics. The following year, he formulated the now-standard interpretation of the probability density function for ψ*ψ in the Schrödinger equation, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1954.

His influence extended far beyond his own research: Max Delbrück, Siegfried Flügge, Friedrich Hund, Pascual Jordan, Maria Goeppert Mayer, Lothar Nordheim, Robert Oppenheimer, and Victor Weisskopf all received their Ph.D. degrees under Born at Göttingen, and his assistants included Enrico Fermi, Werner Heisenberg, Gerhard Herzberg, Friedrich Hund, Wolfgang Pauli, Léon Rosenfeld, Edward Teller, and Eugene Wigner.
In January 1933, when the Nazi Party came to power in Germany, Born, who was born into a Jewish family, was suspended from his professorship at the University of Göttingen. He emigrated to the United Kingdom, where he took a job at [St John's College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Cambridge "St John's College, Cambridge"), and wrote a popular science book, _The Restless Universe_, as well as _Atomic Physics_, which soon became a standard textbook. In October 1936, he was appointed Tait Professor of Natural Philosophy at the University of Edinburgh, where, working with German-born assistants Ernst Walter Kellermann and Klaus Fuchs, he continued his research into physics. He became a naturalised British subject on 31 August 1939, one day before the German invasion of Poland that triggered World War II in Europe. He remained in Edinburgh until 1952, when he retired to Bad Pyrmont, West Germany, and died in a hospital in Göttingen on 5 January 1970.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Born#cite_note-nbwdis-4)

In 1954, physicist Max Born received the Nobel Prize in Physics, sharing the honor with Walther Bothe for their groundbreaking contributions to quantum mechanics. At the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm, Born delivered a heartfelt and thought-provoking speech that remains timeless in its relevance.
Born began by expressing profound gratitude for the recognition, emphasizing the collective spirit of science:
"We are a great fellowship, men of all nations seeking after the truth."
This statement highlighted the global and collaborative essence of scientific exploration—a principle he saw endangered by the growing politicization of science.
Born championed the idea that science thrives on freedom, cautioning against the subjugation of scientific research to political agendas. He lamented barriers of "fear and suspicion" that hindered collaboration among scientists, urging the world to preserve the liberty that allows ideas to flourish.
The Shift in Thinking: From Determinism to Probability
Born's most profound reflections came when he addressed the transformative nature of his work. At the end of the 19th century, scientists viewed the universe as a perfect machine governed by deterministic laws. If one knew the universe's state at a given moment, they believed, its future could be predicted with certainty.

"A philosophy in which the notions of chance and freedom are fundamental seems to me preferable to the almost inhuman determinism of the previous epoch."

He also expressed regret over the absence of his co-laureate, Walther Bothe, who was unwell, and extended heartfelt wishes for his recovery—a reminder of the humility and camaraderie that defined Born's character.
